propositions.text: Ms. Lin applies for judicial review of the Visa Officer's October 8, 2020 decision refusing her study permit and declaring inadmissibility for misrepresentation.
propositions.quote: Kai Hou Lin (Ms. Lin) brings an application for judicial review pursuant to s. 72(1) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act, SC 2001, c 27 [IRPA] of the October 8, 2020 decision of a Visa Officer, stationed at the Consulate General of Canada in Hong Kong.

propositions.text: Visa Officer refused Ms. Lin's study permit and declared her inadmissible for five years for misrepresentation under para. 40(1)(a) IRPA.
propositions.quote: The Visa Officer refused Ms. Lin’s application for a study permit and declared her inadmissible to enter Canada for a period of five years on the grounds of misrepresentation, pursuant to para. 40(1)(a) of the IRPA.

paragraphs.summary: The court states Ms. Lin applies for judicial review of the Visa Officer's refusal and inadmissibility decision for misrepresentation.

propositions.text: The application for judicial review is dismissed for reasons set out below.
propositions.quote: For the reasons set out below, I dismiss the application for judicial review.

paragraphs.summary: The court dismisses the application for judicial review.

propositions.text: Ms. Lin is a Taiwanese citizen accepted into Concordia University's MA Educational Studies program on March 6, 2020.
propositions.quote: Ms. Lin is a citizen of Taiwan. On March 6, 2020, she received a letter from Concordia University advising her that she had been accepted into the Master of Arts Educational Studies program.

paragraphs.summary: The court states Ms. Lin is Taiwanese and was accepted into Concordia University's MA program on March 6, 2020.

propositions.text: In May 2020, Ms. Lin engaged regulated consultant Yang to assist with her study permit application, signing a declaration of truthful answers.
propositions.quote: In and around May 2020, Ms. Lin engaged the services of YANG Jingci (“Yang”), a regulated Canadian Immigration Consultant to assist with the study permit application (the “application”). The Use of A Representative Form signed by Ms. Lin on or about May 24, 2020 reads in part as follows: I declare that I have fully and truthfully answered all questions on this form and any Attached Application (if applicable); I also declare that I have read and understood all the statements on this form, having asked and obtained an explanation for every point that was not clear to me.

paragraphs.summary: The court states Ms. Lin hired consultant Yang in May 2020 and signed a declaration of truthful answers on the application form.

propositions.text: Yang submitted Ms. Lin's application on June 1, 2020, answering 'no' to prior visa denial or entry refusal question.
propositions.quote: On or about June 1, 2020, Yang submitted the application, dated May 27, 2020, to Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada (the “IRCC”). Ms. Lin, through her agent Yang said “no” to the following question: “Have you ever been denied a visa or permit, denied entry or ordered to leave Canada or any other country or territory?” (the “relevant question”).

paragraphs.summary: The court states Yang submitted the application on June 1, 2020, answering 'no' to prior visa denial or entry refusal question.

propositions.text: IRCC received the application June 2, 2020, noting Ms. Lin's 'no' answer contradicted information about prior US removal and entry denial.
propositions.quote: On or about June 2, 2020, the IRCC received Ms. Lin’s Application. In the process of reviewing the Application, a Visa Officer noted that Ms. Lin had answered “no” to the relevant question. The response was contrary to information in the possession of IRCC which demonstrated that Ms. Lin had previously been removed from the United States, and denied entry to the United States and its’ territory of Guam.

paragraphs.summary: The court states IRCC received the application June 2, noting Ms. Lin's 'no' answer contradicted prior US removal and entry denial info.

propositions.text: On June 11, 2020, IRCC sent a procedural fairness letter raising concerns about truthful answers and prior US immigration encounters, allowing response within 90 days.
propositions.quote: On June 11, 2020, the IRCC sent a procedural fairness letter to Ms. Lin advising her that it had concerns that she had not truthfully answered all questions in her Application, noting her encounters with the US Immigration Authority. The IRCC provided Ms. Lin an opportunity to respond to the concerns raised and to submit additional material if necessary.

paragraphs.summary: The court states IRCC sent a June 11 procedural fairness letter raising concerns about truthful answers and prior US immigration encounters.

propositions.text: On August 18, 2020, Ms. Lin, via solicitor, admitted prior US immigration encounters were accidentally omitted by consultant Yang, who admitted error.
propositions.quote: On August 18, 2020, in response to IRCC’s procedural fairness letter, Ms. Lin, through her solicitor, admitted to her previous encounters with US Immigration and stated they were accidently omitted by Yang, her immigration consultant. Yang had previously reported this omission as early as July 8, 2020 in the following language: For the background question “Have you ever been refused a visa or permit, denied entry or ordered to leave Canada or any other country or territory?”, I had checked “NO” without verifying this with the Applicant, and without letting her review the form before submission.

paragraphs.summary: The court states Ms. Lin admitted prior US immigration encounters were accidentally omitted by consultant Yang, who admitted error.

propositions.text: Ms. Lin admitted US removal in 2008, inadmissibility for 5 years, visa denial in 2013 due to Guam visit, and expressed regret for omission.
propositions.quote: Ms. Lin admitted that she was removed from the United States on March 29, 2008 for not being in possession of the proper paperwork, and that, as a result, she became inadmissible to the United States for 5 years. Additionally, Ms. Lin admitted that in November 2013, her United States’ visa application was denied because she had attempted to visit the United States territory of Guam in November 2011. Ms. Lin expressed regret and apologized for her “innocent omission”.

paragraphs.summary: The court states Ms. Lin admitted US removal in 2008, 5-year inadmissibility, 2013 visa denial, and expressed regret for omission.

propositions.text: Visa Officer reviewed Ms. Lin's response, rejected innocent mistake claim, found it unreasonable not to review application, and concluded misrepresentation was intentional and material.
propositions.quote: On or about October 8, 2020, a visa officer reviewed Ms. Lin’s response to the procedural fairness letter. The Visa Officer considered Ms. Lin’s contention that the misrepresentation had been an innocent mistake made by her previous representative. The Visa Officer rejected that contention. The Visa Officer concluded it was unreasonable for Ms. Lin not to review the Application for accuracy before submitting it. Moreover it was unreasonable that someone who was previously banned for 5 years from the United States would “somehow forget to disclose” it on the Application. Recall that the previous immigration issues included deportation from the United States, a refusal to enter Guam in 2011 and a refusal to enter the United States in 2013. Based on a review of the file, the Visa Officer determined that the misrepresentation was intentional and the information was material since it could have led to an error in the administration of the IRPA.

paragraphs.summary: The Visa Officer rejected Ms. Lin's innocent mistake claim, found misrepresentation intentional and material.

propositions.text: Relevant IRPA provisions are ss. 11(1), 16(1), 40(1)(a) and 40(2).
propositions.quote: The relevant provisions are ss. 11(1), 16(1), 40(1)(a) and 40(2) of the IRPA as set out in the Schedule below.

paragraphs.summary: The court states the relevant IRPA provisions are ss. 11(1), 16(1), 40(1)(a) and 40(2).

propositions.text: Ms. Lin alleges breach of procedural fairness; Minister says it is a new issue not raised in leave application and should not be heard.
propositions.quote: Ms. Lin contends she is the victim of a breach of procedural fairness. The Minister contends the alleged breach of procedural fairness is a new issue, which was not raised in the leave application for judicial review and ought not to be heard.

propositions.text: Court will examine if procedural fairness issue is new, if it should be allowed, and if Visa Officer breached procedural fairness.
propositions.quote: This Court will examine whether the issue of procedural fairness constitutes a “new issue”, whether it should allow such an issue to be raised in the present application, and, in the affirmative, whether the Visa Officer did, in fact, breach procedural fairness.

paragraphs.summary: Ms. Lin alleges breach of procedural fairness; Minister says it's a new issue; court will examine these questions.

propositions.text: Ms. Lin argues Visa Officer's decision is unreasonable; her failure to disclose was innocent omission by representative.
propositions.quote: Ms. Lin also contends that the Visa Officer’s decision is unreasonable, alleging that there was proof that her failure to disclose her previous encounters with the US Immigration Authority is based on an innocent omission from her representative.

propositions.text: Court will examine if innocent misrepresentation exception applies and if Visa Officer's intentional misrepresentation finding is reasonable.
propositions.quote: This Court will examine whether the innocent misrepresentation exception applies in the present circumstances, and will consequently determine whether the Visa Officer’s conclusion that Ms. Lin’s misrepresentation was intentional is reasonable.

paragraphs.summary: Ms. Lin argues Visa Officer's decision is unreasonable due to innocent omission; court will examine this and the Visa Officer's finding.

propositions.text: Standard of review for Visa Officer's decision is reasonableness, per Vavilov 2019 SCC 65 at para 25.
propositions.quote: Ms. Lin and the Minister agree that the applicable standard of review of the Visa Officer’s decision is reasonableness (Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration) v Vavilov, 2019 SCC 65, 441 DLR (4th) 1 at para 25).

paragraphs.summary: The court states the standard of review is reasonableness per Vavilov 2019 SCC 65.

propositions.text: Procedural fairness issues are reviewed for correctness, assessing if fairness level was met (Khosa 2009 SCC 12 at para 43).
propositions.quote: Procedural fairness issues are subject to a correctness review. The Court is to determine whether the process followed by the decision-maker satisfied the level of fairness required in all of the circumstances (Canada (Citizenship and Immigration) v Khosa, 2009 SCC 12, [2009] 1 SCR 339 at para 43).

paragraphs.summary: The court states procedural fairness issues are reviewed for correctness per Khosa 2009 SCC 12.

propositions.text: Ms. Lin says she was not made aware of misrepresentation concerns or consequences in procedural fairness letter, denying meaningful response opportunity.
propositions.quote: Ms. Lin contends she was not made aware of concerns about misrepresentation pursuant to para. 40(1)(a) of the IRPA or their consequences, in the procedural fairness letter. She says that she was not afforded a meaningful opportunity to respond to the Visa Officer’s concerns expressed in the Visa Officer’s notes.

propositions.text: Ms. Lin argues misrepresentation finding, causing visa denial and 5-year inadmissibility, requires higher procedural fairness degree (Asanova 2020 FC 1173 at para 30).
propositions.quote: She argues that a finding of misrepresentation, which not only denies the visa, but also makes her inadmissible to Canada for five years, warrants a higher degree of procedural fairness (Asanova v Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration), 2020 FC 1173 [Asanova] at para 30).

paragraphs.summary: Ms. Lin argues she lacked awareness of misrepresentation concerns and that misrepresentation findings require higher procedural fairness.

propositions.text: Ms. Lin relies on Ge 2017 FC 594: officers must put truthfulness concerns to applicants and allow response before denial and inadmissibility finding.
propositions.quote: Ms. Lin relies on Ge v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2017 FC 594, wherein the Court concluded that if an officer has a concern that an applicant is not being truthful in his or her responses, the officer has an obligation to put this concern to the applicant and provide an opportunity to respond, before denying the application and finding the applicant inadmissible to enter Canada.

paragraphs.summary: Ms. Lin relies on Ge 2017 FC 594 that officers must notify applicants of truthfulness concerns and allow response before denial.

propositions.text: Minister says procedural fairness issue is new, raised first in Ms. Lin's further memorandum, not in leave application.
propositions.quote: The Minister says that the issue of procedural fairness is a new one raised by Ms. Lin in her further memorandum. The Minister contends the new issue could not have been reasonably anticipated since Ms. Lin’s notice of application for judicial review, the supporting affidavits and the memorandum at leave are silent on that issue.

paragraphs.summary: The Minister argues procedural fairness issue is new and was not raised in the leave application.

propositions.text: Al Mansuri 2007 FC 22 sets factors for allowing new issues in further memoranda: facts availability, prejudice, record completeness, relation to granted issues, strength, delay.
propositions.quote: In Al Mansuri v Canada (Public Safety and Emergency Preparedness), 2007 FC 22, 315 FTR 1 at para 12 [Al Mansuri], this Court sets out a non-exhaustive list of factors relevant to the exercise of discretion about whether to allow issues to be raised for the first time in a party’s further memorandum of fact and law: were all the facts and matters relevant to the new issues (or available with reasonable diligence) at the time the leave application was filed; is there any suggestion of prejudice to the opposing party if the new issue is considered; does the record disclose all of the facts relevant to the new issue; is the new issue related to those in respect of which leave was granted; what is the apparent strength of the new issue; and will allowing the new issue to be raised unduly delay the hearing.

paragraphs.summary: The court cites Al Mansuri 2007 FC 22 factors for allowing new issues in further memoranda.

propositions.text: The procedural fairness breach is a new issue not raised at leave, but discretion favors allowing it as facts exist, no prejudice, no delay, and Minister can respond.
propositions.quote: I am satisfied the alleged breach of procedural fairness is a new issue. It was not raised in the leave application, nor was it addressed in the leave submissions. The judge who heard the leave application could only grant leave on the strength of the application before him or her. However, when I consider the Mansuri test, I see no reason why I should not exercise my discretion in favour of allowing the issue of procedural fairness to be raised. All of the facts necessary to resolve that issue are found in the Certified Tribunal Record. The issue is one that is regularly argued before this Court in connection with such applications for judicial review. The Minister is, in my view, not prejudiced and has had ample opportunity to respond to the allegations. Finally, allowing the new issue to be raised will not result in any delay in the hearing or disposition of this matter.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds procedural fairness breach is a new issue but allows it due to available facts, no prejudice, and no delay.

propositions.text: Procedural fairness owed to study permit applicants is low even with misrepresentation and inadmissibility issues
propositions.quote: The Minister contends that the procedural fairness owed to an applicant seeking a study permit is at the lower end of the spectrum, even where issues of misrepresentation arise and a potential order of inadmissibility arises (Tuiran v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2018 FC 324 [Tuiran] at paras 14 and 19).

propositions.text: Procedural fairness requirements were met regardless of whether a higher or lower degree is owed
propositions.quote: For the reasons set out below, I am satisfied that the requirements of procedural fairness were met in the circumstances, whether one accepts that a higher degree of procedural fairness is owed to the applicant (Asanova at para 30) or a lower one (Tuiran at para 14).

paragraphs.summary: The respondent argues procedural fairness owed is low; the court finds procedural fairness requirements were met regardless of degree owed.

propositions.text: Procedural fairness letter stated Visa Officer's concern about failure under s.16 IRPA related to US Immigration encounters
propositions.quote: The procedural fairness letter clearly stated the Visa Officer’s concern that Ms. Lin had failed to meet her obligation under s. 16 of the IRPA. The Visa Officer specifically stated that the concerns related to Ms. Lin’s previous encounters with the United States Immigration Authority.

propositions.text: Absence of reference to para. 40(1)(a) IRPA did not breach procedural fairness
propositions.quote: The absence of any reference to para. 40(1)(a) of the IRPA, regarding the possible consequences of the failure to answer truthfully, did not breach Ms. Lin’s right to procedural fairness.

propositions.text: Letter set out concerns and notified Ms. Lin of the case she had to meet
propositions.quote: The letter set out the Visa Officer’s concerns and notified Ms. Lin of the case she had to meet.

propositions.text: Ms. Lin's reply to procedural fairness letter cited Koo v Canada
propositions.quote: Ms. Lin’s reply to the procedural fairness letter cites Koo v Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration), 2008 FC 931, [2009] 3 FCR 446 [Koo].

propositions.text: Koo involved refusal for misrepresentation under para. 40(1)(a) IRPA and inadmissibility
propositions.quote: In Koo, the applicant’s permanent resident visa application was refused on the basis that he had misrepresented or withheld material facts within the meaning of para. 40(1)(a) of the IRPA.

propositions.text: Koo applicant retained consultant and was declared inadmissible for 5 years
propositions.quote: Like Ms. Lin, Mr. Koo had retained the services of a consultant to prepare and submit his application. The Visa Officer had concerns that Mr. Koo had not disclosed material facts. Consequently, his application for permanent residence was refused and he was declared inadmissible to Canada for 5 years.

propositions.text: Ms. Lin knew or ought to have known consequences of para. 40(1)(a) IRPA from her response and Koo reference
propositions.quote: Given her response to the procedural fairness letter and her reference to Koo, it is clear Ms. Lin knew or ought to have known the consequences of para. 40(1)(a) of the IRPA.

propositions.text: No breach of procedural fairness found
propositions.quote: I am satisfied that there was no breach of procedural fairness.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the procedural fairness letter properly stated concerns; Ms. Lin knew consequences of para. 40(1)(a) IRPA; no breach of procedural fairness.

propositions.text: Visa Officer failed to provide rational reasons for concluding omission was intentional
propositions.quote: Ms. Lin submits that the Visa Officer failed to provide rational reasons for concluding that her “innocent omission” was intentional.

propositions.text: Proof of innocence includes application not signed by her and consultant admitted submitting without her confirmation
propositions.quote: According to her, proof of the innocence of the misrepresentation is evidenced by the fact the Application was not signed by her and the fact her immigration consultant admitted submitting the Application without providing her an opportunity to confirm its accuracy.

paragraphs.summary: Ms. Lin argues the Visa Officer lacked rational reasons to find intentional omission, citing unsigned application and consultant's admission.

propositions.text: Two-part test for innocent misrepresentation: subjective honest belief and objective reasonableness
propositions.quote: In Alkhaldi v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2019 FC 584 at para 19, this Court sets out the two part test necessary to establish the innocent misrepresentation exception: The subjective test where the decision-maker asks whether or not the applicant honestly believed he/she was not making a misrepresentation; and The objective test, where the decision-maker asks whether or not it was reasonable on the facts that the applicant believed he/she was not making a misrepresentation.

paragraphs.summary: The court cites Alkhaldi for the two-part test for innocent misrepresentation: subjective honest belief and objective reasonableness.

propositions.text: Ms. Lin admitted omission was unintentional but gave little explanation
propositions.quote: Although Ms. Lin admitted to the omission and stated that it was unintentional, she provides little explanation as to how the error came about and why she did not review the application.

propositions.text: Visa Officer did not accept 'forgot to disclose' and held Ms. Lin responsible for accuracy even if submitted by representative
propositions.quote: The Visa Officer did not accept that Ms. Lin “just forgot to disclose her travel history” and determined that she was responsible for ensuring that the Application was accurate and correct, even if it was submitted by a representative on her behalf.

propositions.text: Visa Officer found it was not objectively reasonable that Ms. Lin believed she was not misrepresenting
propositions.quote: Moreover, the Visa Officer found that it was not objectively reasonable that Ms. Lin would believe that she was not making a misrepresentation.

paragraphs.summary: Ms. Lin admitted unintentional omission but gave little explanation; Visa Officer rejected 'forgot' excuse and found belief not objectively reasonable.

propositions.text: Visa Officer's decision aligns with jurisprudence on misrepresentation and innocent misrepresentation exception
propositions.quote: The Visa Officer’s decision is consistent with the jurisprudence regarding misrepresentation and the innocent misrepresentation exception.

propositions.text: Applicants have duty of candour to provide complete, accurate, honest information (Kazzi, Goudarzi)
propositions.quote: This Court has repeatedly stated that an applicant has a duty of candour, and is to provide complete, accurate, honest and truthful information when applying for entry to Canada (Kazzi v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2017 FC 153 at para 38; Goudarzi v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2012 FC 425 at para 40).

propositions.text: Para 40(1) IRPA applies even if third party misrepresents material fact (Wang)
propositions.quote: Moreover, this Court has found that where a third party misrepresents a material fact, para 40(1) of the IRPA still applies (Wang v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2015 FC 647 at para 25).

propositions.text: Applicant responsible for application content; belief of no misrepresentation unreasonable if application not reviewed (Goburdhun, Haque)
propositions.quote: An applicant is always responsible for the content of their application, and the belief that he or she was not misrepresenting a material fact is not reasonable where they fail to review their application and ensure its completeness and veracity (Goburdhun v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2013 FC 971, 439 FTR 210 at para 28; Haque v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2011 FC 315 at para 16).

paragraphs.summary: The Visa Officer's decision aligns with case law requiring candour; applicants responsible for application content even if third party errs.

propositions.text: Innocent misrepresentation exception is narrow, applies only in extraordinary circumstances
propositions.quote: The innocent misrepresentation exception is very narrow and only applies to truly extraordinary circumstances.

propositions.text: Applicant must show honest and reasonable belief of no misrepresentation and lack of control over knowledge (Patel, Ahmed)
propositions.quote: An applicant must demonstrate that he or she honestly and reasonably believed that they were not misrepresenting a material fact and that knowledge of the misrepresentation was beyond the applicant’s control (Patel v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2017 FC 401 at para 64; Ahmed v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2020 FC 107 at para 32).

paragraphs.summary: The court explains the narrow scope of the innocent misrepresentation exception and its requirements.

propositions.text: Ms. Lin signed Use of Representative Form declaring truthfulness of application
propositions.quote: Ms. Lin signed the Use of a Representative Form in which she declared the truthfulness of that set out in the form and any attached application.

propositions.text: Ms. Lin had high duty to ensure accuracy of attached application
propositions.quote: The application for a study permit was, in this case, the attached application. She, having made a declaration in the Use of a Representative Form, had a high duty to ensure the accuracy of the attached form.

propositions.text: Ms. Lin had experience with US immigration and knew or ought to have known duty of candour
propositions.quote: She, having had experience successfully entering the United States, and having been deported from the United States and refused entry twice to that country and its territories, knew or ought to have known the extremely high duty of candour owed to immigration authorities.

propositions.text: Innocent mistake exception to s.40 IRPA not applicable; Visa Officer's decision reasonable
propositions.quote: I am satisfied the innocent mistake exception to s. 40 is not applicable and the decision is reasonable.

propositions.text: Visa Officer reasonably concluded Ms. Lin failed to show honest and reasonable belief or lack of control over misrepresentation
propositions.quote: The Visa Officer’s conclusion that Ms. Lin failed to demonstrate that she honestly and reasonably believed that she was not misrepresenting a material fact, or that it was beyond her control, is reasonable.

paragraphs.summary: Ms. Lin signed a declaration and had duty to ensure accuracy; Visa Officer reasonably found innocent mistake exception inapplicable.

propositions.text: Visa Officer's decision meets reasonableness standards from Vavilov and Dunsmuir
propositions.quote: The Visa Officer’s analysis meets all the hallmarks of reasonableness, including those set out in Vavilov at para 85, and Dunsmuir v New Brunswick, 2008 SCC 9, [2008] 1 SCR 190 at paras 47 to 49.

propositions.text: Decision is internally coherent, rational, justified, transparent, intelligible and defensible
propositions.quote: Namely, the Visa Officer’s decision is “based on an internally coherent and rational chain of analysis” and is “justified in relation to the legal and factual constraints that bear on the decision”. It can also be said that the Visa Officer’s decision is transparent and intelligible, falling “within a range of possible, acceptable outcomes which are defensible in respect of the facts and the law”.

propositions.text: Reviewing court must defer to administrative decision-maker's reasonable decision
propositions.quote: In such circumstances, a reviewing court must defer to the administrative decision-maker’s decision.

paragraphs.summary: The Visa Officer's decision is reasonable, coherent, justified, and the court must defer to it.

propositions.text: Application for judicial review is dismissed
propositions.quote: I dismiss the within application for judicial review.

paragraphs.summary: The court dismisses the application for judicial review.

propositions.text: Application dismissed without costs
propositions.quote: The application for judicial review is dismissed without costs.

propositions.text: No question certified for Federal Court of Appeal as no serious question of general importance
propositions.quote: I conclude there is no serious question of general importance which would be dispositive of this matter on appeal (s. 74(d) of the IRPA; Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration) v Zazai, 2004 FCA 89, 318 NR 365 at para 11). It follows that no question is certified for consideration by the Federal Court of Appeal.

propositions.text: No question certified for Federal Court of Appeal
propositions.quote: No question is certified for consideration by the Federal Court of Appeal.

paragraphs.summary: The court dismisses the application without costs and refuses to certify any question for appeal.
